newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Markets aid ABN profit, outlook cloudy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Markets aid ABN profit, outlook cloudy.

text.p: Soaring securities markets helped ABN AMRO NV unveil a 26 percent increase in 1996 net profit on Thursday but the Dutch banking giant gave mixed signals about its prospects for 1997.
In a flurry of announcements, ABN AMRO also said it planned a four-for-one share split and a buy-back of one percent of its shares as part of a planned listing in New York.
Net profit rose to 3.30 billion guilders ($1.7 billion) from 2.62 billion in 1995 and the dividend was raised to 4.20 guilders per share from 3.60 previously.
"1996 was an excellent year for the bank. All businesses contributed to the strong result," ABN AMRO said.
Profits were in line with analysts' forecasts but the shares weakened after the bank declined to make a forecast for the current year due to uncertainty about financial markets.
The shares stood at 140.40 guilders at 1405 GMT, down two guilders from Wednesday's close.
The annual results included the first disclosure of the bank's hidden reserves, which totalled 4.02 billion guilders at the end of 1996.
ABN AMRO said total revenue rose 18 percent to 19.0 billion guilders in 1996, with the largest component, net interest revenue, increasing by 12.6 percent.
Interest margins were squeezed by strong competition but this was more than offset by volume growth, particularly in the United States, where ABN AMRO is the largest foreign bank.
"But we also have cream on top of the cake -- commissions and financial transactions," chairman Jan Kalff told reporters.

Financial transactions income soared 57 percent to 1.88 billion guilders and net commissions gained 19 percent to 4.96 billion, mainly due to buoyant stock markets and growth in asset management fees.

ABN AMRO set aside provisions of 340 million guilders to adapt computer software for the advent of a single European currency in 1999 and the millennium, projects which it said would cost a total of 500 million guilders over time.
The bank said it was optimistic about its outlook but it was too early to make a forecast of current year results.
"That doesn't mean we would expect a decrease in profits. It's simply not possible to give any statement about the future," Kalff said.
But, echoing the views of U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan, Kalff said uncertainty about future trading had increased in the last six months due to the high level of stock markets.
He said a fall in equity markets would affect the bank's provisions and could have an indirect effect on the general direction of financial markets. "That's a bit worrying," Kalff said.
ABN also said it planned to list its shares in American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) on the New York Stock Exchange, improving its ability to raise capital from U.S. investors.
Rival Dutch banking and insurance group ING Groep NV, which announces 1996 results next month, has previously announced a New York listing for this year.
As part of the listing, ABN AMRO will buy back one percent of its own shares, which it will re-offer to U.S. investors.
The bank also announced plans for a four-for-one share split to reduce the price and increase the liquidity of its shares.
Analysts welcomed the results but were not surprised by the bank's caution about the future.
Peter Thorne of Paribas Capital Markets said Kalff was right to be suspicious of whether the strong increases in commission and trading income which buoyed 1996 results could be repeated in 1997.
"It's a fabulous set of numbers. They have clearly done well from the securities markets...but it's not clear they can do better next year," he said.
CSFB analyst Mark Hoge said he was disappointed with the low dividend payout ratio of 45 percent.
"With that, and the comments from Kalff, you could make a pessimistic case," he said.
But Ton Gietman of HSBC Van Meer James Capel said the bank's decision to omit a forecast should not be seen as bearish.
"That's a normal cautious statement," he said.
